title: Practice: Effect of Concentration on Rate

questions.stem: A student reacts magnesium ribbon with three different concentrations of HCl: 0.5, 1.0, and 2.0 mol/dm³. She plots volume of H2 produced against time. Which observation about the three curves is correct?

options.text: All three curves start at the same steepness and reach different final volumes
Higher concentration gives a steeper initial curve but all reach the same final volume (if Mg is limiting)
Higher concentration gives a less steep curve because the reaction finishes sooner
The curves are identical because the same mass of magnesium is used

questions.explanation: Higher concentration means faster initial rate (steeper curve) because there are more HCl particles per unit volume, so collisions with Mg are more frequent. If magnesium is the limiting reactant in all cases, the same final volume of H2 is produced - it just takes longer to reach completion with lower concentrations.

questions.stem: In the sodium thiosulfate and HCl reaction (disappearing cross experiment), a student uses 1.0 mol/dm³ acid and records a time of 40 seconds. She repeats with 2.0 mol/dm³ acid. What would you expect?

options.text: Exactly 20 seconds, because double concentration halves the time
About 80 seconds, because higher concentration slows the reaction
Approximately 20 seconds, because the rate roughly doubles with doubled concentration
40 seconds, because concentration does not affect this reaction

questions.explanation: Doubling the concentration approximately doubles the rate, which approximately halves the time (since rate is inversely proportional to time in this experiment). The time would be approximately 20 seconds. It may not be exactly 20 seconds because the relationship is not always perfectly proportional, but it should be close.

questions.stem: During a reaction in solution, the rate decreases over time even though the temperature remains constant. Using concentration to explain, why does this happen?

options.text: The catalyst is being used up
The products inhibit the reaction
As reactants are used up, their concentration decreases, reducing collision frequency
The activation energy increases as the reaction proceeds

questions.explanation: As the reaction progresses, reactant particles are converted to products. The concentration of reactants decreases over time. With fewer reactant particles per unit volume, collisions occur less frequently, so the rate decreases. This is why rate-time curves are steep at the start (high concentration) and flatten later (low concentration).

questions.stem: For the reaction between sodium thiosulfate and hydrochloric acid, a student plots 1/time (a measure of rate) against concentration of sodium thiosulfate. The graph is a straight line through the origin. What does this show?

options.text: Rate is inversely proportional to concentration
Rate is directly proportional to concentration
Rate does not depend on concentration
Time is directly proportional to concentration

questions.explanation: A straight line through the origin on a graph of rate (1/time) against concentration shows that rate is directly proportional to concentration. When concentration doubles, the rate doubles. This is consistent with collision theory - doubling the number of particles doubles the collision frequency.

questions.stem: A factory increases the concentration of a reactant to speed up production. What is a potential safety concern with this change?

options.text: The reaction might become endothermic
Higher concentration means a faster, possibly dangerously vigorous reaction that could overheat or produce gas too quickly
Higher concentration always causes an explosion
Higher concentration makes the products less pure

questions.explanation: Increasing concentration increases the reaction rate, which could lead to a dangerously vigorous reaction. For exothermic reactions, heat may be produced faster than it can be dissipated, causing overheating. For gas-producing reactions, pressure could build up dangerously. Industrial processes must balance reaction rate with safety considerations.
